lessonRef.title: Close reading with evidence: close reading how an author uses reasons and evidence for a point

studentTask.text: This Grade 4 lesson develops close reading how an author uses reasons and evidence for a point within the unit “Opinion and Argument: Reasons, Evidence, and Fair Reading.” Read the delivered Academy-original source before responding. Strong ELA work separates what the source explicitly says from what a reader infers, selects evidence because it is relevant and sufficient, and explains the connection instead of leaving a quotation to speak for itself. Today's close reading with evidence work asks you to make that reasoning visible and to revise if the evidence does not support the first idea.

sourceReference.text:
The Millbrook branch library should extend its weekday hours from five o'clock to seven o'clock.

My strongest reason is that the current schedule excludes the households the library was built to serve. According to the branch's own 2025 service report, 61 percent of Millbrook residents work shifts ending at five o'clock or later. A library that locks its doors at five is open to the community only during the hours most of the community is unavailable.

My second reason is that the demand is already visible in the branch's numbers. The same report shows that the final hour of operation, four to five o'clock, accounts for 24 percent of weekday visits, more than any other single hour. When a service is busiest at the moment it shuts down, that is evidence of demand that is being cut off rather than demand that has been met.

My third reason is that the fixed costs are already paid. The building, the collection, the computers, and the internet connection cost the same whether the doors are open at six o'clock or locked. Extending hours purchases additional public use of an asset the public has already bought.

Some residents argue that the money would be better spent on new books rather than on staffing two extra hours. This is a fair objection, and it is not based on a misunderstanding. A collection that never grows does eventually stop drawing readers.

I would answer it this way. A book that cannot be borrowed because the building is closed provides no service at all, and 61 percent of residents currently cannot borrow it on a weekday. Expanding access to the entire existing collection reaches more readers than adding a small number of new titles to a collection most residents cannot get to.

The books are already on the shelves. The question is who is allowed through the door.

guidedSupport.text:
Use this source-specific routine for “A Case for Later Library Hours”:
1. Preview the title and paragraph structure; write what close reading how an author uses reasons and evidence for a point asks you to notice or do.
2. Mark one statement the source makes explicitly and one inference a reader could draw. Keep the two kinds of thinking separate.
3. Test the inference with the evidence requirement in today's task. If the evidence is weak or incomplete, narrow or revise the inference.
4. Draft your own response. A facilitator may clarify directions or ask questions, but may not supply your claim, evidence choice, sentences, or revision.

independentEvidenceTask.text:
Read “A Case for Later Library Hours,” then answer: Read the source without interruption, then decide which detail most changes an interpretation of close reading how an author uses reasons and evidence for a point. Explain the change.

Deliverable: Grade 4: an evidence log and a short interpretation; write one organized paragraph.

Evidence requirement: Use two exact details. Label source evidence with a paragraph number or another precise location. Your response must explain the connection between the evidence and your conclusion.

remediation.text:
If close reading how an author uses reasons and evidence for a point is not yet secure, return to “A Case for Later Library Hours” before starting over:
- Evidence gap: underline the exact words that support the idea and label their paragraph or location.
- Reasoning gap: complete the stem “This evidence matters because …” in your own words, then reread the question.
- Overclaim: name what the source does not establish and narrow the conclusion to what the evidence can support.
- Completion gap: compare the draft with each learner success criterion and repair one missing part at a time.

extension.text: Apply close reading how an author uses reasons and evidence for a point to a different paragraph or a defensible alternative interpretation of “A Case for Later Library Hours.” Compare the new result with your first response and explain which evidence changes, which reasoning still holds, and why.
